title: Chickamauga Cherokee
summary: After the 1775 Sycamore Shoals sale, Dragging Canoe led Cherokee who rejected it to Chickamauga Creek, resisting settler expansion until 1794.
bodyMarkdown:
In March 1775, at Sycamore Shoals on the Watauga River, [Richard Henderson](/stories/richard-henderson/)'s [Transylvania Company](https://grokipedia.com/page/Transylvania_Colony) bought Cherokee claims to roughly 20 million acres, much of it the Kentucky hunting ground. Older Overhill leaders agreed to the sale, but Cherokee custom expected broad consent for land cessions. Many younger Cherokee saw the deal as giving away the land their people depended on.

The best-known opponent was the war chief [Dragging Canoe](https://grokipedia.com/page/Dragging_Canoe), called Tsiyu Gansini in Cherokee and a son of the diplomat [Attakullakulla](https://grokipedia.com/page/Attakullakulla). He argued that settlers would keep coming and that only armed resistance could hold them back. When American militias burned many Overhill towns in the [Cherokee–American wars](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cherokee%E2%80%93American_wars) of 1776, he and his followers refused the peace that other towns accepted.

In the winter of 1776–77 they moved down the [Tennessee River](https://grokipedia.com/page/Tennessee_River) and built new towns along Chickamauga Creek, near present-day Chattanooga. American settlers began calling them the [Chickamauga Cherokee](https://grokipedia.com/page/Chickamauga_Cherokee). After Virginia and North Carolina militia struck those towns in 1779, they moved farther downriver to the Five Lower Towns, including Running Water and [Nickajack](https://grokipedia.com/page/Nickajack).

The Chickamauga were never only Cherokee. Allied Creeks and Shawnees joined them, along with some white frontiersmen and escaped Africans, and they drew supplies from British and later Spanish agents. Their warriors struck the Cumberland settlements and East Tennessee, and they ambushed migrant parties on the [Wilderness Road](https://grokipedia.com/page/Wilderness_Road) into Kentucky. Militia raids in return killed many people on both sides.

Dragging Canoe died on March 1, 1792, at Running Water, soon after a diplomatic mission to the Chickasaw. Leaders such as John Watts carried on the fight. In September 1794 Southwest Territory militia burned Nickajack and Running Water, and later that year the Treaty of Tellico Blockhouse ended organized Chickamauga resistance.

For Kentucky, the Chickamauga wars were part of the price of the Transylvania sale. The same purchase that opened the Wilderness Road also split the Cherokee Nation and set off nearly twenty years of war along the southern approaches to the new settlements.

## Kentucky today

The Wilderness Road still runs through Cumberland Gap National Historical Park, where trails trace the route that migrants and warriors both used. Kentucky has no federally recognized Cherokee nation today, but the Cherokee Nation, the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians and the United Keetoowah Band all trace their history to the people who argued over Sycamore Shoals.
